sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they are marketed as premium, high‑performance solutions for specific, well‑defined use cases (e.g., metal fabrication, CNC machining), because hobbyists value quality and reliability over cost. Who benefits: Hobbyists and small workshop owners who need reliable, accurate tools for specific tasks.. Why behaviour changes: If Gühring positions its tools as essential for professional‑grade results, hobbyists will perceive them as a necessary investment rather than a discretionary purchase.. How value is captured: Gühring would sell under its own brand at premium prices, capturing margin through direct‑to‑consumer sales or through authorized distributors who can emphasize quality.. Assumptions: Hobbyists have sufficient disposable income to afford premium tools for specific tasks.; They are willing to pay more for tools that deliver consistent precision.; Marketing can effectively communicate the tool’s performance benefits to this segment.. Predictions: Surveyed hobbyists will indicate intent to purchase Gühring tools for specific use cases at a price 20‑30% above standard industrial tools.; Pilot sales of a limited consumer line will generate at least 10% of total Gühring revenue within 12 months.; Customer satisfaction scores for the consumer line will be comparable to or exceed those of established hobbyist brands..

T2: Gühring will capture consumer demand by leveraging its existing B2B distribution network to offer a limited consumer line through existing partners, avoiding the need for new channels, because the partners already reach hobbyists and small workshops. Who benefits: Gühring benefits from partner sales and margin without new marketing or distribution costs; partners gain access to premium tools for their customer base.. Why behaviour changes: Partners already serve hobbyists and small workshops; if Gühring provides them with a premium, differentiated product, partners will promote it to their existing customer base, creating demand without Gühring needing to build a new consumer. How value is captured: Gühring sells under partner brands or through partner channels, earning margin on each unit sold while leveraging existing distribution relationships.. Assumptions: Partners have existing customer segments that include hobbyists and small workshops.; Partners are willing to promote Gühring tools as premium, differentiated offerings.; The tools meet partner expectations for quality and performance.. Predictions: Partner sales of Gühring tools will increase by at least 15% within 12 months compared to baseline.; Partner satisfaction with Gühring tools will be high enough to encourage further promotion.; Consumer awareness of Gühring will rise among partners’ existing hobbyist customers without dedicated marketing..

case.question: Should Rieter Holding AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing short-staple spinning machines, components and after-sales services for industrial spinning mills? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small-scale creators will adopt Rieter’s entry-level spinning machines because they need affordable automation to speed their creative process, and Rieter’s existing expertise in textile calculations makes the machines more appealing. Who benefits: Hobbyists, hand spinners, and small-space creators who want to produce yarn for personal projects.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently face high entry barriers (cost, learning curve) and limited options. A low‑cost, automated spinning solution would reduce time and effort, making it worthwhile to switch from manual methods.. How value is captured: Rieter would sell the Artisan line directly to consumers at a modest margin, leveraging its existing textile calculator brand trust to differentiate the consumer proposition.. Assumptions: Hobbyists are willing to invest in equipment that reduces project time.; The market for entry‑level spinning machines exists and is large enough to justify production.; Rieter can adapt its existing technology (e.g., carding, drawing) to a consumer‑friendly package.. Predictions: If offered, hobbyists will purchase the Artisan line at a rate sufficient to achieve a positive return on investment within 12 months.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong craft and textile communities (e.g., Europe, North America)..

T2: Eco‑conscious consumers will adopt Rieter’s entry‑level spinning machines because they seek sustainable, recycled yarn production, and Rieter’s existing GRS certification and recycling capabilities make the machines a credible green choice. Who benefits: Consumers who prioritize sustainability and recycled materials for personal projects.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers currently face limited options for affordable, recycled yarn and are willing to invest in equipment that aligns with their environmental values.. How value is captured: Rieter would market the Artisan line as a sustainable, recycled spinning solution, commanding a premium price and leveraging its GRS certification to differentiate the consumer proposition.. Assumptions: Eco‑conscious consumers are willing to pay more for recycled yarn products.; The market for affordable, sustainable spinning equipment exists and is large enough to justify production.; Rieter can communicate its recycling capabilities effectively to consumers.. Predictions: If offered, eco‑conscious consumers will purchase the Artisan line at a rate sufficient to achieve a positive return on investment within 12 months.; Sales will be concentrated in regions with strong sustainability awareness (e.g., Europe, North America)..

Test "Hobbyist vs Eco Consumer Preference Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either hobbyist-focused or eco-focused messaging.. Sample: 500 respondents recruited from craft and sustainability-focused online communities (e.g., craft yarn forums, sustainability blogs) who have indicated interest in spinning or yarn production.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy at price X") and willingness to pay (WTP) for the Artisan line presented with the corresponding messaging.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for hobbyist-focused messaging than for eco-focused messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for eco-focused messaging than for hobbyist-focused messaging.. Decision rule: If the difference in purchase intent between the two messaging conditions exceeds 10 percentage points, proceed to develop the corresponding consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 5 percentage points, conclude that. Cost: 12000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Conduct the proposed Hobbyist vs Eco Consumer Preference Test (or a smaller pilot) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for hobbyist-focused messaging before committing resources. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Value proposition: A low‑cost, automated spinning solution leveraging Rieter’s existing textile calculator brand trust to differentiate the consumer proposition.. Favoured theory: T1. Would change if: If the test shows a 10‑percentage‑point or greater difference in purchase intent between hobbyist and eco messaging, proceed to develop the corresponding consumer proposition.; If the test shows no significant difference or purchase intent below 5‑percentage points, conclude that there is insufficient evidence to justify investment and maintain the status quo.. Who benefits: Consumers seeking efficient home storage and willingness to pay for convenience; Kardex would capture value through higher‑margin consumer sales and subscription services.. Track daily active users, refund redemption frequency, and subscription retention rate.. If the data+subscription pilot shows a statistically significant (p<0.05) higher subscription retention rate than the control group (e.g., >=10% higher), proceed with the bundled subscription model. If both. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Measure: Primary outcome: average purchase intent score (1‑10) for each framing condition. Secondary outcomes: average maximum price willing to pay and average recommendation likelihood.. T1: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a convenient, high-performance solution for a specific use case that is easy to use and offers measurable benefits (e.g., faster installation, superior durability). Who benefits: DIY homeowners and small contractors who need reliable, out-of-the-box solutions for common home improvement tasks.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers believe the product meets or exceeds professional standards and reduces installation time or complexity, they will choose it over generic alternatives, even at a premium price.. How value is captured: Sika can charge premium prices for branded, consumer-friendly products and sell through retail channels, capturing margin on each unit while leveraging existing distribution networks.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay more for perceived quality.; Retail partners will stock Sika consumer products if they demonstrate clear performance advantages.; Marketing can effectively communicate the differentiated use case and benefits to DIY buyers.. Predictions: In a test offering a differentiated consumer product (e.g., a DIY waterproofing kit) in a retail setting, purchase intent or actual sales will be higher than for a generic competitor product.; Surveyed consumers will rate the product’s ease of use and perceived performance at least 10% higher than alternatives..

T2: Consumers will adopt a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safe, low-risk solution that minimizes the chance of installation errors or performance failures, reducing perceived risk compared to generic alternatives. Who benefits: DIY homeowners who are hesitant to tackle complex projects and prefer products that promise minimal risk of damage or failure.. Why behaviour changes: If consumers view the product as virtually foolproof and backed by a reputable brand, they will choose it even at a higher price, because they avoid the cost and frustration of mistakes.. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Method: Randomized controlled trial offering two consumer propositions: 1) a home reverse vending machine for plastic bottle recycling with cash refund, 2) a subscription-based sorting service using TOMRA sensors for home waste sorting. Participants are randomly assigned to either the home machine (Group A) or the subscription service (Group B). Both groups receive a brief explanation of the offer and a link to a registration page. After 4 weeks, we track the number of units registered (. Sample: 2,000 households in a mid-size U.S. city with significant consumer recycling activity. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Digital Refund Convenience Test" between T1; T2. Method: Run a 12‑week pilot in a mid‑size city (e.g., 200,000 residents) offering two versions of a digital refund app: (1) a basic version with 10% digital refund and drop‑off at a nearby collection point; (2) a premium version with 10% digital refund and drop‑off from home via a mobile app. Track weekly drop‑off numbers for each version. Also collect survey data on perceived convenience (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (binary).. Sample: 2,000 residents who have used a reverse vending machine in the past 12 months, recruited via local panels and social media.. Measure: Number of containers dropped off per week for each version; average convenience score; proportion of participants who would pay a premium for home drop‑off.. Predictions: T1: The basic version will achieve at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7; the premium version will achieve at least 300 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 8.; T2: The premium version will achieve at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7; the basic version will achieve fewer than 300 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score below 7.. Decision rule: If the premium version achieves at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7, proceed to develop a full consumer proposition for home drop‑off. If the basic version achieves at least 500 drop‑offs per week and a convenience score above 7, proceed to develop a full consumer proposition for collection points. If neither version meets the threshold, conclude there is. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: Over the last few years, the spinning industry has continued to move to Asia. As a consequence, Rieter, the leading supplier of systems for short-staple fibre spinning, has made significant investments in China and India adding production capacities in these countries.
The world market for staple fiber machines relevant to Rieter has an annual volume of CHF 2 200 million to CHF 4 000 million. Rieter is the market leader with a share of about 30 percent.

Owing to extraordinary restructuring expenses and transaction costs in connection with the acquisition of Barmag in the amount of CHF 54.2 million, Rieter closed the 2025 financial year with a net loss of CHF 63.4 million (2024: net profit of CHF 10.4 million).

Why behaviour changes: Consumers and businesses are increasingly demanding sustainable and eco-friendly products. By offering specialized spinning solutions for sustainable fibers, Rieter can attract environmentally conscious customers and command a premium price. Sample: 100 individual buyers: 50 current industrial spinning mill customers, 50 potential textile manufacturers focusing on sustainability (new market segment). Measure: 1.  Willingness to pay a premium for: (a) specialized spinning solutions (b) sustainable spinning solutions 2.  Current use of sustainable fibers 3. Interest in switching to Rieter's offerings. For over 30 years, FoodSaver has introduced innovative vacuum sealers, bags, and accessories to help people around the world avoid food waste, enjoy their food at its freshest, and save thousands of dollars each year.
Baseline chamber machines are therefore the ideal vacuum packaging solution for butchers´shops, restaurants, hotels, chees dairies, direct marketing companies and farm shops.

The bacterium Clostridium botulinum is able to grow and produce a harmful toxin in the absence of oxygen. It is important that vacuum-packed chilled foods have the necessary controlling factors or hurdles in place to minimise the risk of growth and toxin production by this organism, throughout the shelf-life of the product.

MULTIVAC tabletop chamber machines can be used very flexibly due to their compact dimensions. This means they are an ideal packaging solution for butchers, cheese dairies, restaurants, hotels, direct sellers and supermarkets as well as for a wide range of consumer goods.

sources.excerpt: In light of the current transformation in the beverage and liquid-food industry as well as rising demands for sustainable, competitive and efficient products, Krones is restructuring its profitable and growing Compact Class line of business, which delivers machines and lines for the small and medium output range.

Krones AG traditionally uses the BrauBeviale specifically to unveil new equipment for small and mid-tier breweries. In recent years, the number of craft breweries has risen spectacularly worldwide. So Krones’ exhibits are designed to meet the needs of this sector as well.
The home beer brewing machine market size was estimated at USD 213.4 million in 2025 and is expected to reach USD 237.9 million in 2026.

With the aid of our innovative, value-added solutions, our dense global service network and reliable completion of projects for our international customers, we are able to obtain adjusted prices despite the cost trend. Despite the ongoing intense competition for orders, we are sticking to our disciplined price strategy.

The company is headquartered in Neutraubling, Germany, and employs over 21,000 people worldwide. Consolidated sales in 2025 totalled 5.663 billion euros. Around 90 per cent of Krones’ products are sold abroad.
It is the ideal brewing device for switching from hobby to commercial brewing, for example as an introduction for caterers who want to offer their own beer to their guests.

2024 was the first year since 2005 that the number of breweries that closed outpaced brewery openings nationwide. Yet, the total number of breweries in the U.S. increased to 9,922, up from 9,838 in 2023. Over the year, 430 new breweries opened while 529 closed.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Professional vs Retail Pricing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two identical Biesse CNC machines: one presented as a professional-grade tool priced at 15% above current professional models, and one presented as a retail-priced model available through major online marketplaces at a price 15% below professional models. Participants indicate purchase intent (1-10) and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale. The test runs for 12 weeks, with 500 participants per condition (1,000 total).. Sample: 500 DIY enthusiasts recruited via hobbyist forums and 500 retail shoppers recruited via general consumer panels, balanced for age, gender, and self-reported CNC experience.. Measure: Purchase intent score (1-10) and WTP difference between professional and retail versions.. Predictions: T1: Professional version will achieve a higher purchase intent and WTP than the retail version, because consumers value professional-grade accuracy and are willing to pay more for it.; T2: Retail version will achieve a higher purchase intent and WTP than the professional version, because consumers prefer convenience and lower price points, and can buy through familiar retail channels.. Decision rule: If the professional version’s average purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than the retail version, T1 is supported. If the retail version’s average purchase intent score is at least 1.5 points higher than the professional version, T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Low-Cost Cable Offering" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Participants view a product description of a Lapp-branded cable for home automation (e.g., EV charging, smart home). The description emphasizes either premium positioning (safety, reliability, industrial reputation) or low-cost positioning (price discount, industrial scale). Participants indicate whether they would purchase the cable and the maximum price they would pay. The test is run with 500 private drivers (private EV owners, DIY enthusiasts) in Germany.. Sample: 500 German private drivers (private EV owners, DIY enthusiasts) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and region.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and maximum price willing to pay (EUR).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants exposed to the premium description will indicate purchase intent, and their average maximum price will be at least 20% above competitor pricing.; T2: At least 40% of participants exposed to the low-cost description will indicate purchase intent, and their average maximum price will be at least 10% below competitor pricing.. Decision rule: If the premium group meets its threshold (purchase intent ≥ 30% and average price ≥ 20% premium) and the low-cost group does not meet its threshold (purchase intent ≥ 40% and average price ≥ 10% discount), conclude that the premium proposition aligns with T1. If both meet their thresholds, conclude that both strategies can work and further testing is needed. If neither meets its threshold, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Participants are recruited from hobbyist CNC forums (e.g., Tormach, CNCZone) and offered a Gühring drill bit at a price 10‑20% below its usual retail price (e.g., €150 instead of €180). They are asked to indicate whether they would purchase it and, if so, the maximum price they would pay. The test runs for 4 weeks, with 200 participants expected to complete the survey.. Sample: 200 hobbyists who have posted about CNC projects in the past 12 months, recruited via forum announcements and social media.. Measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willing to pay (EUR). Secondary measure: self‑reported importance of compatibility with existing CNC machines (1‑5 scale).. Predictions: T1: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and compatibility will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 60% of those who would buy.; T2: At least 30% of participants will indicate purchase intent at the discounted price, and brand prestige will be ranked as the top purchase driver for at least 40% of those who would buy.. If neither condition is met, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 4 weeks.

case.question: Should MULTIVAC Sepp Haggenmüller SE & Co. KG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing packaging machines and processing equipment for food, medical and industrial producers? What evidence would justify that investment?

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the running-cost offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Chamber vacuum sealers, while representing a smaller market share, are gaining popularity among serious home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who require professional-grade sealing capabilities for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing.

T1: Serious home cooks and food enthusiasts will purchase MULTIVAC vacuum chamber machines for sous vide cooking and bulk food processing because they value professional-grade sealing performance and the ability to achieve airtight, mess-free results. Who benefits: Home cooks and culinary enthusiasts who prepare gourmet meals for family or friends, and who are willing to invest in premium kitchen equipment for quality control.. Why behaviour changes: These consumers prioritize food freshness and safety, and they appreciate the precision control that chamber sealers provide for temperature and pressure, enabling better outcomes for sous vide and bulk food storage.. How value is captured: MULTIVAC would capture value by selling direct to consumers through online channels or specialty retailers, pricing at a premium justified by performance, and earning recurring revenue from consumables (bags, accessories).. Assumptions: Home vacuum sealing demand exists beyond the 30% market share of commercial users.; Consumers are willing to pay €200-€500 for a tabletop chamber sealer.; Distribution can reach this segment through e-commerce or specialty kitchen retailers.. Test "Digital Refund vs Tangible Reward Consumer Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Run two identical pilot sites in the same geographic area (e.g., a shopping mall) for 12 weeks. Both sites offer a TOMRA consumer RVM with a mobile app for drop‑off and digital refund. In Site A, the refund is paid directly via the app (no retailer partner). In Site B, the refund is linked to a retailer‑specific loyalty program that offers points redeemable for discounts at that retailer. Track the number of containers returned per week and the redemption rate of points (if any).. Sample: Each site serves approximately 5,000 unique shoppers per week (total 10,000 per 12 weeks).. Measure: Return rate per week (containers dropped off) and redemption rate of retailer points (if applicable).. Predictions: T1: Site A return rate will be at least 15% higher than baseline RVM return rates in comparable locations (e.g., 15% vs 10%).; T2: Site B redemption rate will be at least 15% higher than baseline RVM redemption rates for existing retailer‑linked programs (e.g., 15% vs 10%).. Decision rule: If Site A return rate ≥ 15% and Site B redemption rate ≤ 10%, conclude T1 is better supported. If Site A return rate ≤ 10% and Site B redemption rate ≥ 15%, conclude T2 is better supported. If both rates meet thresholds, both theories remain plausible. If neither meets thresholds, the evidence is insufficient to justify expansion.. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Subscription Pricing" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to two product descriptions and pricing options. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in Switzerland who report limited storage space and interest in home organization. They are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) Premium home storage system (description emphasizing space‑saving, modern design, and price at 1.5x the baseline price of a comparable manual. Sample: 200 participants (100 per condition). Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 0‑10 scale ("Would you buy this product?") and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as the maximum price they would pay.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show higher purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because consumers value premium, space‑saving solutions and are willing to pay more for perceived value.; T2: Condition A will show lower purchase intent and WTP than Condition B, because consumers prefer subscription service that reduces upfront cost and provides convenience.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10 percentage points AND the average WTP in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 10% (e.g., Condition A WTP = 120% of baseline price, Condition B WTP = 90% of baseline price), then T1 is supported. If the. Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage, emphasizing premium, space‑saving design and convenience, and test demand through a controlled survey experiment. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE concerns a rental versus purchase choice for a compact automated storage module, not consumer demand for premium home storage. It does not address T1’s core premise that consumers value premium, space‑saving design and are willing to pay a premium price. Therefore T1 remains unchanged. New claim: Consumers will adopt Kardex’s automated storage solutions for home use if they perceive the system as a premium, space‑saving product that reduces clutter and increases productivity, and if price aligns with perceived value.. Evidence: SYN-KARDEX-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for home storage, emphasizing premium, space‑saving design and convenience, and validate demand through a controlled survey experiment. Target customer: Homeowners in Switzerland and nearby markets who report limited storage space and interest in home organization, particularly tech‑savvy, urban residents.. Value proposition: A Kardex‑branded automated storage system that combines space‑saving design, proven performance, and a subscription‑based service model to reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing support.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (200 participants, 8 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium‑priced home storage system versus a subscription‑based model.. Uncertainty: Consumer willingness to pay a premium price for home storage; the size of the addressable market; competitive response from established consumer storage brands; and the feasibility of delivering a subscription‑based service at scale.. Would change if: If the test shows purchase intent for the premium offering is at least 10 percentage points higher than for the subscription offering, and willingness to pay is at least 10% higher, confidence in T1 would increase.; If the test shows strong preference for the subscription model (e.g., higher intent and willingness to pay for a lower‑priced offering), T2 would become more plausible.; If no significant difference is observed between the two offerings, the case for either theory would weaken.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential deposit return if they perceive a convenient, immediate digital refund and a clear map to collection points, because they value the ease of refunding containers without retailer involvement. Who benefits: Individual consumers receiving digital refunds quickly and easily.. Why behaviour changes: The removal of retailer obligations in some jurisdictions (e.g., New South Wales DRS) creates a demand for consumer‑friendly refund mechanisms; consumers are accustomed to app‑based digital payouts and will switch if they see the same. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value by charging consumers a small fee for each container deposited and by selling data on recycling volume to municipalities or manufacturers.. Assumptions: Consumers trust that digital refunds will be honored.; There is sufficient consumer awareness and access to the app in target markets.; Competition from other refund mechanisms (e.g., cash redemption) is limited.. Predictions: A test group offered the app will show a higher proportion of containers deposited compared to a control group without the app.; Surveyed consumers will rate the app’s ease of refund as “very easy” or “easily possible” at a rate above 60%..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine for residential deposit return if they receive a tangible reward (e.g., points, discounts, or loyalty credits) that can be redeemed for goods or services, because they value the additional incentive beyond the refund. Who benefits: Individual consumers receiving a tangible reward.. Why behaviour changes: Tangible rewards create a direct financial benefit that motivates consumers to actively return containers, especially when combined with convenience (e.g., app‑based deposit tracking).. How value is captured: TOMRA captures value by partnering with retailers or service providers to offer rewards, and by selling aggregated recycling data to manufacturers or municipalities.. Assumptions: Consumers trust that rewards will be honored and are aware of redemption options.; Retailers or service providers are willing to partner to offer rewards.; Competition from cash redemption or other refund mechanisms is not sufficient to offset the reward incentive.. Predictions: A test group offered a reward system will show a higher proportion of containers deposited compared to a control group without rewards.; Surveyed consumers will rate the reward system as “very attractive” or “easily attractive” at a rate above 55%..

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Digital Refund vs Environmental Reward Choice Experiment" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with simulated consumer scenarios. Participants view a description of a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) offering either a digital refund (cash refund via app) or a tangible environmental reward (points/discounts). They choose which option they would select. The experiment also collects demographic data and willingness‑to‑pay information.. Sample: 500 Norwegian consumers recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and recycling behavior.. Measure: Choice proportion (digital refund vs environmental reward) and willingness‑to‑pay (maximum amount participants would pay for the service).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the digital refund option, and willingness‑to‑pay will be below €5 per transaction.; T2: At least 60% of participants will choose the environmental reward option, and willingness‑to‑pay will be above €5 per transaction.. Decision rule: If the observed choice proportion for the digital refund option is at least 60% and willingness‑to‑pay is below €5, proceed with developing a consumer‑facing digital refund RVM. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Hobbyist Tools" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from hobbyist forums and CNC enthusiast communities. They are shown a product description of a Gühring drill bit for metalworking, emphasizing its precision, quality, and reliability. They are then asked: "How much would you be willing to pay for this drill bit?" (open‑ended price). The survey also captures demographic data (age, gender, primary use case).. Sample: 200 participants (100 per arm) recruited via hobbyist forums and CNC communities. Randomly assigned to either a Gühring‑branded proposition (T1) or a licensed third‑party proposition (T2).. Measure: Average willingness‑to‑pay (EUR) for the simulated product.. Predictions: T1: Average willingness‑to‑pay for Gühring‑branded proposition will be at least 15% higher than for the third‑party proposition.; T2: No significant difference in willingness‑to‑pay between the two arms, or the third‑party proposition will show a higher willingness.. Decision rule: If the Gühring‑branded average willingness‑to‑pay exceeds the third‑party average by ≥ 15% (p≥ 0.05), proceed with the Gühring consumer proposition (support T1). If the difference is <15%, proceed with the licensing model (support T2). If no. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small workshops, leveraging Gühring’s existing B2B distribution channels to reach individual buyers. Begin with a limited launch of a consumer‑branded drill bit for metalworking, priced at a modest premium, and measure willingness‑to‑pay through a controlled survey before scaling. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing errors and does not address consumer demand, pricing, or willingness to pay for Gühring tools. Therefore it does not affect T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small workshops, leveraging Gühring’s existing B2B distribution channels to reach individual buyers. Begin with a limited launch of a consumer‑branded drill bit for metalworking, priced at a modest premium, and measure willingness‑to‑pay through a controlled survey before scaling. Target customer: Individual hobbyists and small workshops (home CNC users) who need reliable metalworking tools for precision projects.. Value proposition: A Gühring‑branded drill bit that delivers the same professional quality and precision as its industrial tools, but priced affordably for hobbyists, while leveraging Gühring’s reputation and existing B2B channels to reach them.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed consumer willingness‑to‑pay survey (200 participants, 100 per arm) to compare Gühring‑branded and third‑party propositions. Use the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with the consumer proposition or license the. Uncertainty: The actual price sensitivity of hobbyists and small workshops, the size of the addressable market, and the competitive response from other brands are uncertain. The survey will resolve this.. Would change if: If the survey shows willingness‑to‑pay for the Gühring‑branded proposition is <15% higher than the third‑party proposition, supporting T1 and justifying investment.; If the survey shows no significant difference or the third‑party proposition outperforms, shifting support to T2 and recommending licensing instead.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s tools if they perceive them as affordable, reliable, and easy to use for precision metalworking, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Individual hobbyists and small metalworking shops that need reliable tools for precision cuts.. Why behaviour changes: These users currently avoid Gühring due to perceived high cost and lack of consumer-friendly branding. If Gühring offers a lower-priced, easy-to-purchase line with clear DIY applications, they will switch from generic or competitor brands.. How value is captured: Gühring would sell directly to consumers through an online shop or retail partners, capturing higher margins than B2B sales while leveraging existing manufacturing capacity.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops are willing to pay a premium for quality but are deterred by high prices and lack of consumer-friendly channels.; Gühring can adapt its existing tools (e.g., drills, cutters) to meet hobbyist needs without major redesign.; A consumer brand or clear DIY messaging will differentiate Gühring from competitors in the hobbyist market.. Predictions: If Gühring launches a consumer line with clear DIY messaging and affordable pricing, purchase intent among hobbyists will increase compared to a control group.; Sales through direct-to-consumer channels will grow faster than B2B sales in the first year, indicating successful capture of the hobbyist segment..

T2: Gühring can capture hobbyist demand by leveraging its existing B2B distribution network to offer consumer-friendly bundles or subscription services, avoiding the need for a separate consumer brand. Who benefits: Gühring benefits from higher volume sales and reduced marketing costs; hobbyists gain access to quality tools through existing channels.. Why behaviour changes: Hobbyists currently avoid Gühring due to high prices and lack of consumer-friendly channels. Offering bundles or subscriptions through existing B2B partners would lower friction and make Gühring accessible without rebranding.. How value is captured: Gühring would sell bundles or subscriptions directly to consumers via B2B partners, capturing higher margins than bulk B2B sales while leveraging existing distribution.. Assumptions: Hobbyists are willing to pay a premium for quality tools if they can obtain them through familiar B2B channels.; Gühring’s B2B partners are willing to promote consumer bundles to their customer base.; Bundling or subscription pricing can be structured to be attractive to hobbyists without cannibalizing premium B2B sales.. Test "Consumer vs B2B Bundle Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled experiment.. Sample: 200 hobbyists/small workshops (recruited via metalworking forums and social media) and 100 B2B procurement managers from automotive/aerospace/engineering firms.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: would buy) and stated willingness to pay for a Gühring drill bit at a price point of €150. Secondary measure: preferred channel (direct-to-consumer vs B2B bundle).. Predictions: T1: At least 55% of hobbyists will indicate purchase intent and willingness to pay €150 for a Gühring drill bit sold directly via an online shop.; T2: At least 55% of B2B procurement managers will indicate purchase intent and willingness to pay €150 for a Gühring drill bit bundled through their existing B2B partner, and at least 30% of hobbyists will indicate purchase intent for the same bundle.. Decision rule: If hobbyists’ purchase intent for direct-to-consumer sales ≥ 55% and B2B bundle intent ≤ 30%, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If B2B bundle intent ≥ 55% and direct-to-consumer intent ≤ 30%, proceed to develop a B2B bundle/subscription model (supports T2). If both meet thresholds, consider a hybrid approach. If neither meets thresholds, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

It does not address hobbyist demand, pricing, or direct-to-consumer channels, so it does not affect T1. New claim: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s tools if they perceive them as affordable, reliable, and easy to use for precision metalworking, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.. Evidence: SYN-GUEHRING-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists and small workshops, sold directly via an online shop with clear DIY messaging and affordable pricing. Begin with a limited launch of a single product line (e.g., a set of precision drills) to test demand before scaling. Target customer: Individual hobbyists and small metalworking shops (1-10 employees) who need reliable, affordable tools for precision cuts.. Value proposition: High-quality, precision metalworking tools marketed as easy-to-use DIY products, sold at a price point that aligns with hobbyist budgets, with clear instructions and support through Gühring’s existing online shop.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed choice-based conjoint survey (200 hobbyists/small workshops and 100 B2B procurement managers) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a Gühring drill bit at €150, and compare against thresholds for proceeding.. Uncertainty: The size of the hobbyist market and their willingness to pay for Gühring tools are uncertain; the survey results will resolve this. The B2B bundle option remains uncertain due to lack of evidence on partner willingness and hobbyist interest. Would change if: If the survey shows hobbyist purchase intent below 55% or B2B bundle intent above 55%, the recommendation would shift to favor the corresponding alternative (e.g., B2B bundle). If both meet thresholds, a hybrid model would be considered.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

events.text: Objective: Determine whether Biesse S.p.A. should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current B2B offerings, and identify evidence that would justify such an investment.. Constraints: Limited to public sources; internal financial and contractual details may not be available.; Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.; Current revenue is predominantly from abroad; any new consumer proposition must consider existing B2B relationships and market presence.; Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, and a viable route to individual buyers for the proposed use case.. Participants view two product descriptions: a premium Biesse consumer CNC machine (high accuracy, professional-grade, €2,500 price) and an affordable Biesse consumer CNC machine (same accuracy, €1,200 price). They are asked to indicate willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale and purchase intent (1‑10).. Sample: 300 DIY woodworkers and homeowners recruited via panel, balanced for age, gender, and self‑reported experience with CNC machines.. Measure: Average WTP difference between premium and affordable versions (points). Purchase intent difference (points).. Predictions: T1: Premium version WTP ≥ 15% above affordable version; purchase intent for premium version ≥ 10% higher.; T2: Affordable version WTP ≥ 15% below premium version; purchase intent for affordable version ≥ 10% higher.. Decision rule: If premium WTP ≥ 15% above affordable WTP, proceed with premium consumer proposition. If affordable WTP ≥ 15% below premium WTP, proceed with affordable volume proposition. If neither condition met, no expansion recommended.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. Test "Subscription vs Premium Integrated Purchase Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice experiment with a sample of 200 small brewers and batch producers (recruited via industry forums and social media). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: (A) Subscription model: monthly fee for a brewhouse with scheduled maintenance and service; (B) Premium integrated purchase: one-time purchase of a Krones integrated brewhouse with no upfront cost. Both scenarios describe the same brewhouse (CRAFT-STAR 20hl) with identical performance claims (downtime reduction, yield increase). Participants choose which. Sample: 200 small brewers and batch producers (100 per arm) recruited via industry forums and social media. Measure: Choice: Subscription (A) vs Premium Purchase (B). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7-point scale (1‑ €2,000‑ €4,000).. Predictions: T1: At least 60% of participants will choose the premium purchase (B) and indicate a WTP of at least €2,500, indicating they value reliability and are willing to pay for it.; T2: At least 60% of participants will choose the subscription (A) and indicate a WTP of at least €1,500, indicating they prefer lower upfront cost and cash‑flow flexibility.. Decision rule: If the proportion choosing premium purchase (B) ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €2,500, proceed to develop a premium integrated consumer proposition. If the proportion choosing subscription (A) ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €1,500, proceed to develop a subscription/leasing model. If neither condition is met, conclude that. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited households in a deposit-return scheme were assigned equally to two offers for returning empty containers. Both paid the identical deposit refund into the same app, with the same fee and payout time. One offer collected bagged containers from the household's door every two weeks; the other asked the household to drop the same bags at a return point in a nearby store. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a bonus. The outcome was a paid sign-up still active after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 active sign-ups for the doorstep-collection offer and 72 for the store drop-off offer. This tests whether the return trip changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that collection could be run at that fee, how store partners would respond, or that households would pay for anything beyond the refund. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product listing and pricing. Participants are recruited from hobbyist forums and metalworking communities. They are shown a Gühring precision tool (e.g., a drill bit) described as suitable for their hobby projects, with three price points: a premium price (e.g., 25% above competitor), a consumer-friendly price (e.g., 10% above competitor), and a B2B price (same as current online shop). Participants indicate whether they would purchase at each price point and. Sample: 300 hobbyists (150 per price point) recruited via hobbyist forums and metalworking groups. Randomly assigned to see one of the three price points.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy at this price?") and willingness to pay (WTP) measured as maximum price they would pay.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP at the consumer-friendly price compared to the premium price, indicating hobbyists value reliability and affordability.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP at the B2B price compared to the consumer-friendly price, indicating hobbyists prefer existing procurement channels and are willing to pay a premium for convenience.. Decision rule: If the consumer-friendly price group shows purchase intent ≥ 40% and a WTP ≥ €150 (or ≥ 1.5x competitor price) while the B2B price group shows intent ≤ 30%, then T1 is supported. If the reverse pattern holds, T2 is supported. If both price groups show <30% intent, both theories are rejected.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) to gather direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a differentiated consumer proposition. Until then, maintain the current B2B focus while exploring consumer-friendly packaging through existing B2B channels as a secondary path. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Run the proposed Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test (X1) to gather direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for a differentiated consumer proposition. Until then, maintain the current B2B focus while exploring consumer-friendly packaging through existing B2B channels as a secondary path. Target customer: Hobbyists and small workshops (DIY metalworkers) who currently use generic tools or lower-quality precision tools and need reliable, affordable tools for home or small workshop projects.. Value proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that offers precision metalworking tools with proven reliability, affordable pricing, and packaging that fits existing B2B procurement workflows (PunchOut, OCI).. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on hobbyist demand and willingness to pay for Gühring tools. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Direct-to-Consumer vs. Aftermarket Price Sensitivity Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are recruited from Italy, Germany, and the United States (markets with strong motorcycle/off-road culture). They are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium direct-to-consumer (DTC) offer for a Brembo brake kit (e.g., €750 for a motorcycle kit). Group B sees the same kit priced at €250 (aftermarket price). Both groups are asked: "Would you purchase this kit at the offered price?" (yes/no).. Sample: 300 participants (100 per group). Participants are screened for self-identified motorcycle/off-road enthusiasts (e.g., have ridden for >5 years, own a motorcycle/off-road vehicle).. Measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage of participants who select "yes" to the DTC offer).. Predictions: T1: Group A will show a purchase intent rate of at least 30% (indicating willingness to pay premium for a branded DTC kit).; T2: Group B will show a purchase intent rate of at least 30% (indicating willingness to pay aftermarket price for a branded DTC kit).. Decision rule: If Group A’s purchase intent rate ≥ 30% and Group B’s ≤ 20%, proceed to develop a differentiated DTC proposition targeting enthusiasts. If both rates ≤ 20%, no expansion. If Group A ≥ 30% and Group B ≥ 30%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Home brewers and small-batch producers will adopt Krones equipment if they perceive it as a scalable, cost-effective way to increase production capacity and achieve consistent quality, because they need to meet growing demand for unique, limited-edition brews. Who benefits: Individual brewers and small-batch producers who want to scale production without sacrificing product quality.. Why behaviour changes: These producers currently use small-batch equipment or manual methods that limit output and consistency. They will switch to Krones if they believe the equipment can be easily scaled while maintaining product integrity.. How value is captured: Krones captures value by selling machines and lines that enable higher throughput and by potentially offering consumables or service contracts, leveraging its existing B2B relationships.. Assumptions: Home brewers and small-batch producers have sufficient capital to purchase Krones equipment.; They value consistency and quality over cost.; They are willing to invest in equipment that can be used for multiple product lines.. Predictions: If offered a compact, affordable filling and packaging system, at least 15% of surveyed home brewers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Krones equipment to small-batch producers will increase by at least 10% year-over-year in the next two years..

T2: Home brewers and small-batch producers will adopt Krones equipment if they perceive it as a status symbol and a way to differentiate their products, because they seek to create unique, premium-priced brews that command higher margins. Who benefits: Individual brewers and small-batch producers who want to position their products as artisanal and premium.. Why behaviour changes: These producers currently use generic or off-the-shelf equipment that limits differentiation. They will switch to Krones if they believe the equipment can be used to create visually distinct, high-quality products that attract consumers.. How value is captured: Krones captures value by selling machines that enable unique packaging and branding, and potentially by licensing its design elements or co‑branding partnerships, leveraging its existing B2B relationships.. Assumptions: Home brewers and small-batch producers are willing to invest in equipment that signals quality and uniqueness.; They value differentiation over cost-effectiveness.; They have access to distribution channels that can showcase premium products.. Predictions: If offered a compact, aesthetically distinctive filling and packaging system, at least 10% of surveyed home brewers will express intent to purchase within 12 weeks.; Sales of Krones equipment to small-batch producers will increase by at least 8% year-over-year in the next two years, driven by premium positioning..

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 72 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Lapp Home Automation" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of homeowners in Germany who own electric vehicles and have home charging installations. They are randomly assigned to one of two scenarios: (A) a premium, integrated Lapp-branded home‑automation charging kit (e.g., a cable and connector set marketed as a single, co‑branded product) priced at €250; (B) a generic Lapp cable and connector set (same technical specifications) priced at €150. Both scenarios include a brief product description emphasizing Lapp’s. Sample: 200 participants (100 per scenario) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and EV ownership status.. Measure: Primary outcome: willingness to pay (WTP) difference between the premium integrated kit and the generic kit (WTP premium). Secondary outcomes: purchase intent (binary) and perceived reliability (1‑10 scale).. Predictions: T1: WTP premium ≥ €100 (i.e., participants value the integrated premium kit at least €100 more than the generic kit).; T2: WTP premium ≤ €50 (i.e., participants do not value the integrated premium kit more than the generic kit).. Decision rule: If WTP premium ≥ €100, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting premium, integrated home‑automation charging. If WTP premium ≤ €50, maintain the current B2B focus. If WTP premium is between €50 and €100, conduct a smaller pilot to validate before committing resources.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. Participants are recruited from a panel of homebrewers and small-batch producers. They are shown two product concepts: (1) a premium, single-batch Krones machine marketed as a status symbol for hobbyists; (2) a high-capacity, multi-batch Krones machine marketed for commercial or high-volume production.
