Test "Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated product offering. Participants are recruited from hobbyist metalworking forums and social media groups. They are shown a product description for a Gühring precision drill bit for a specific use case (e.g., metal fabrication). For the premium price group, the price is set at 150% of the average retail price of comparable Gühring bits. For the subscription group, the price is the same but the description includes a monthly maintenance and tool‑update service. Participants are asked: "Would you purchase this tool at the indicated price?" (yes/no).. Sample: 200 hobbyists (100 per group). Recruitment via hobbyist forums and social media to ensure a mix of experienced and novice users.. Measure: Purchase intent conversion rate (percentage of participants who select "yes" for the offered price).. Predictions: T1: Premium price group conversion rate ≥ 30% (higher than the 20% threshold).; T2: Subscription group conversion rate ≥ 30% (higher than the 20% threshold).. Decision rule: If either group meets its respective 30% threshold, the corresponding theory is supported. If neither meets the threshold, both theories are weakened. If both meet the threshold, the test is inconclusive and further evidence is needed.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Premium vs Compliance Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase intent. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two conditions: (A) Premium messaging emphasizing quality, reliability, and reduced production time; (B) Compliance messaging emphasizing regulatory-compliant, easy-to-use equipment. Both conditions describe a Krones homebrew machine at a premium price (e.g., €3,500). After viewing the assigned message, participants indicate purchase intent on a 0‑10 scale and willingness to pay a premium (e.g., 15‑20% above €3,500).. Sample: 200 homebrewers/small‑batch food producers recruited via hobbyist forums and industry lists, balanced for geographic region and experience.. Measure: Purchase intent score (0‑10) and willingness to pay premium (percentage above €3,500).. Predictions: T1: Condition A (Premium messaging) will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium than Condition B (Compliance messaging).; T2: Condition B (Compliance messaging) will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and willingness to pay premium than Condition A (Premium messaging).. Decision rule: If Condition A’s average purchase intent ≥ 7.5 and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15% above €3,500, proceed with premium‑focused consumer proposition. If Condition B’s average purchase intent ≥ 7.5 and willingness to pay premium ≥ 15% above €3,500, proceed with compliance‑focused consumer proposition. If neither condition meets both thresholds, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: (A) heritage/adjustability messaging emphasizing 50‑year motorsport heritage, market‑leading adjustability, and Italian design; (B) safety/durability messaging emphasizing proven off‑road performance, extreme‑condition reliability, and racing pedigree. Predictions: T1: Group A will report a higher average willingness‑to‑pay than Group B because heritage and adjustability justify premium pricing.; T2: Group B will report a higher average willingness‑to‑pay than Group A because safety and durability in extreme conditions justify premium pricing.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average willingness‑to‑pay exceeds Group B’s by at least €150 (a 10% premium over the €750 price point), we conclude T1 is more likely. Test "Hobbyist Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Recruit 200 hobbyists (100 per arm) via metalworking forums and social media. Randomly assign each participant to one of two conditions: Condition A: offer a Gühring drill at a 20% premium price (e.g., €120 instead of €100) with a brief description of precision and durability benefits. Condition B: offer the same drill at the same €100 price with no premium positioning, using the existing B2B online shop’s. Sample: 200 hobbyists (100 per arm). Measure: Purchase intent: binary “Would you buy this drill?” and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 7‑point scale.. Predictions: T1: Condition A will show at least 60% purchase intent and a WTP of at least €110, indicating hobbyists value premium positioning.; T2: Condition B will show at least 60% purchase intent and a WTP of at least €100, indicating they already purchase through B2B channels and price is secondary.. Decision rule: If purchase intent in Condition A ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €110, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition (supports T1). If purchase intent in Condition B ≥ 60% and WTP ≥ €100, proceed with expanding B2B channels (supports T2). If neither condition meets thresholds, no expansion is. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Consumers in small warehouses and home storage will adopt Kardex’s automated storage systems if they perceive a clear cost savings and reduced manual effort, leading them to pay a premium price for a differentiated consumer proposition. Who benefits: Small warehouse operators and homeowners who need efficient inventory management.. Why behaviour changes: When the cost of automation equals or exceeds manual storage costs and the system demonstrably increases throughput and reduces labor, consumers will switch from manual to automated solutions.. How value is captured: Kardex captures value through premium pricing for differentiated consumer kits, service contracts, and recurring maintenance fees.. Assumptions: Consumers calculate total cost of ownership (TCO) including capital expenditure, operational costs, and potential resale value.; Marketing can effectively communicate TCO savings and operational benefits to target consumers.; Regulatory requirements for safety and compliance are met for consumer-grade systems.. Predictions: A test offering a consumer kit at a 20% premium price will achieve at least a 15% conversion rate among target consumers who report manual storage costs above €500 per month.; Surveyed consumers will cite reduced manual effort and improved inventory accuracy as primary drivers of purchase decision..

Why behaviour changes: When the total cost of ownership (TCO) is presented as a monthly subscription with predictable expenses and measurable performance insights, consumers perceive lower risk and higher utility, leading them to choose automated solutions over. How value is captured: Kardex captures value through recurring monthly fees, data-driven service contracts, and upselling of analytics tools.. Assumptions: Consumers value predictable monthly costs over large upfront payments.; Service contracts are easily understood and demonstrate measurable ROI.; Regulatory compliance and safety standards are met for consumer-grade systems.. Predictions: A test offering a subscription kit at a 15% monthly discount compared to a one-time purchase will achieve at least a 20% subscription uptake among target consumers.; Surveyed consumers will cite lower upfront cost and ongoing support as primary reasons for choosing the subscription model..

Who benefits: Home brewers seeking to elevate their hobby to a professional level and Krones AG through premium consumer sales and brand extension.. Why behaviour changes: As brewers increase output, they seek equipment that can handle larger batches without compromising quality, and they value reliability and ease of expansion over premium branding.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Participants are recruited from motorcycle forums and social media groups. They are shown a description of the Brembo GR-PRO brake kit (or a new, fictional XTRA Signature disc for off-road SSVs) and its €750 price point. They are asked: "Would you purchase this kit for your bike?" (Yes/No) and "What is the maximum price you would pay?" (open‑. Sample: 300 participants: 150 self‑identified high‑performance motorcycle enthusiasts (from forums) and 150 off‑road SSV owners (from off‑road forums). Recruitment cost €1,500.. Measure: Primary outcome: proportion of participants who indicate willingness to pay €750 (Yes). Secondary: average maximum price offered (EUR).. Predictions: T1: At least 40% of enthusiasts will indicate willingness to pay €750, and the average maximum price will exceed €700.; T2: At least 40% of off‑road SSV owners will indicate willingness to pay €750, and the average maximum price will exceed €700.. If only one group meets the threshold, only that. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 32 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby and very small craft brewers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact brewing system. Both showed the identical batch size, brewing steps, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included an automated clean-in-place cycle that cleans and sanitises the vessels after each brew; the other required the same cleaning to be done by hand following a written procedure. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 reservations for the automated-cleaning offer and 72 for the manual-cleaning offer. This tests whether the cleaning burden changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that such a system could be built at a price these buyers pay, that the market is large enough, or that it fits Krones' industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Home Spinning Kit Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized messaging and willingness-to-pay (WTP) questions.. Sample: 500 crafters and hobbyists recruited via craft forums and social media, balanced across two groups (250 per group).. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would you buy this kit?") and WTP (EUR).. Predictions: T1: Group seeing "Creative Hobby" messaging will report purchase intent of at least 15% and WTP of at least EUR300; Group seeing "Eco-Friendly" messaging will report purchase intent of at least 10% and WTP of at least EUR400.; T2: Group seeing "Eco-Friendly" messaging will report purchase intent of at least 15% and WTP of at least EUR400; Group seeing "Creative Hobby" messaging will report purchase intent of at least 10% and WTP of at least EUR300.. Decision rule: If either messaging group meets its respective WTP threshold AND its purchase intent exceeds the other messaging group by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop that consumer proposition. If neither meets its WTP threshold, abandon consumer expansion. If both meet. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed Home Spinning Kit Purchase Intent Test to measure consumer demand and willingness to pay for a branded kit. If either messaging group meets its respective WTP threshold and its purchase intent exceeds the other by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If neither meets WTP, abandon consumer expansion. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-RIETER-UPDATE concerns a training-inclusive offer versus a manual-only offer, not consumer demand or willingness to pay for a branded kit. New claim: Consumers will adopt home spinning kits if they view spinning as a creative hobby, and Rieter can capture value by selling branded kits and premium accessories through its own consumer channel.. Recommendation: Run the proposed Home Spinning Kit Purchase Intent Test to measure consumer demand and willingness to pay for a branded kit. If either messaging group meets its respective WTP threshold and its purchase intent exceeds the other by at least 5 percentage points, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If neither meets WTP, abandon consumer expansion. Target customer: Individual crafters and hobbyists who have recently taken up crocheting or other fiber crafts and seek creative DIY experiences.. Value proposition: A branded home spinning kit that simplifies the spinning process, includes easy-to-follow instructions, and can be sold through Rieter’s own consumer channel at a premium price, leveraging the company’s existing documentation and support.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Execute the 12‑week online survey test with 500 crafters, randomizing messaging and measuring purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Automated Home Storage" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description emphasizing either status/modern lifestyle (T1) or functional storage gain (T2). They are asked: "How much would you pay for a Kardex automated home storage system that meets the following description?" They can select a price range (e.g., $1,000–$5,000) and indicate which description they find more important. The survey also collects demographic data (age, income, home ownership status).. Sample: 500 homeowners in the United States, recruited via an online panel, balanced across age groups and income brackets.. Measure: Average price selected for the status‑focused description versus the functional‑storage description, and the percentage of participants who select a price above $2,000 (a threshold reflecting a premium).. Predictions: T1: Average price for status‑focused description will be at least 20% higher than for functional‑storage description, and at least 30% of participants will select a price above $2,000.; T2: Average price for functional‑storage description will be at least 20% higher than for status‑focused description, and at least 30% of participants will select a price above $2,000.. Decision rule: If the average price for status‑focused description exceeds the functional‑storage description by ≥ 20% AND at least 30% of participants select a price above $2,000, then T1 is supported. If the opposite pattern occurs, T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.. Sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE concerns installation friction and does not address consumer purchase drivers (brand trust, performance, compatibility). Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: Consumers will adopt Eberspächer’s differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a premium, reliable solution for a specific use case (e.g., home EV charging comfort), because they trust the brand’s automotive heritage and are willing to pay a premium for performance and safety.. Evidence: SYN-EBERSPAECHER-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium home EV heater versus a specialized compatible heater. If the test meets the 15% threshold for the premium proposition, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise, maintain B2B focus. Target customer: German EV owners planning to install home charging (estimated 300,000 per year, 10% of total EV owners).. Value proposition: A premium, automotive-grade home EV heater that offers superior performance and reliability, marketed as a trusted automotive brand extension.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €18,000 Consumer Preference Test (X1) with 300 German EV owners to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a premium versus a specialized product.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 are uncertain because there is no direct evidence of consumer demand for a premium proposition or for a specialized compatible solution. The test will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the test shows premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the premium proposition (supporting T1).; If the test shows specialized intent ≥ 45% and premium intent ≤ 35%, we would recommend pursuing the specialized proposition (supporting T2).; If neither meets the 15% threshold, we would recommend no expansion and maintain B2B focus.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

case.question: Should Sika AG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing construction chemicals, sealants and adhesives for contractors, distributors and industrial manufacturers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Why behaviour changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. T1: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they perceive a convenient, digital refund mechanism that is easy to use and accessible via a mobile app, because convenience and digital payout reduce friction and increase willingness to return containers. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive digital refunds and can return containers from home, and retailers who gain foot traffic and can brand themselves as eco‑friendly.. Why behaviour changes: Convenience (no need to visit a redemption center) and digital refund (instant payout without cash) lower perceived effort and reduce barriers to participation.. How value is captured: TOMRA can charge a subscription fee for the app and service, or earn revenue from data on consumer return habits that can be sold to retailers or recycling programs.. Assumptions: Consumers trust the app to accurately track returns and provide refunds.; Retailers are willing to partner with TOMRA to offer the service and promote it to customers.; Regulatory frameworks in target markets permit digital refund mechanisms for deposit return.. Predictions: In a test offering the app to a residential building, at least 30% of residents will register and return containers within the first month.; Surveyed satisfaction with the digital refund process will be rated “very satisfied” by at least 70% of users.; Retailers will report increased foot traffic and repeat purchases among customers who use the app for bottle returns..

T2: Consumers will adopt a consumer‑facing reverse vending machine (RVM) for residential deposit return if they receive a tangible cash refund (e.g., a voucher or coin return) that is easily redeemable at nearby retailers, because physical money provides immediate gratification and reduces trust concerns about digital refunds. Who benefits: Individual consumers who receive cash refunds and can redeem them for goods or services, and retailers who gain additional foot traffic and can partner to facilitate redemption.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

case.question: Should Eberspächer Gruppe GmbH & Co. KG develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, beyond its existing exhaust technology, vehicle heaters and thermal management systems for vehicle manufacturers and specialist dealers? What evidence would justify that investment?
case.source_limits: Evidence is limited to the case dossier: each source shows everything the dossier holds for it, often a short excerpt, not the whole original. Results marked simulated are what-if evidence, not real observations.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 32 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs. Compatible Home EV Heater" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a controlled auction mechanism.. Sample: 300 German consumers who own or plan to purchase an electric vehicle (EV) within the next 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and willingness to pay (WTP) for two product concepts: (1) Premium home EV heater (20% price premium over generic alternatives, marketed as automotive-grade, premium performance). (2) Specialized home EV heater (same price as generic alternatives, marketed as the only compatible solution for the EV brand’s charging network).. Predictions: T1: Purchase intent for the premium product will be at least 15% higher than for the specialized product, because consumers trust the automotive brand and are willing to pay a premium for performance and reliability.; T2: Purchase intent for the specialized product will be at least 15% higher than for the premium product, because consumers need compatibility with their specific EV charging setup and value reliability over brand trust.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent ≥ 45% and specialized purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt premium proposition (supports T1). If specialized purchase intent ≥ 45% and premium purchase intent ≤ 35% → adopt specialized proposition (supports T2). If neither meets threshold → no expansion recommended. If both meet threshold →. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer vs Partner Branding Test" between T1; T2. Both listings are promoted via social media and targeted ads to hobbyist CNC users.. Sample: Target 5,000 hobbyist CNC enthusiasts identified through social media groups, DIY forums, and online marketplaces. Recruit 2,000 for each listing (1,000 direct, 1,000 partner).. Measure: Conversion rate (percentage of visitors who place a deposit) and average order value for each listing.. Predictions: T1: The direct listing will convert at least 5% of visitors and have an average order value of €2,500, while the partner listing will convert <3% and have an average order value <€2,000.; T2: The partner listing will convert at least 5% of visitors and have an average order value of €2,500, while the direct listing will convert <3% and have an average order value <€2,000.. Decision rule: If the direct listing converts ≥5% and partner listing converts <3%, proceed with a consumer‑focused direct‑to‑retail proposition (supports T1). If partner listing converts ≥5% and direct listing converts <3%, proceed with a partner‑branded retail proposition (supports T2). If both listings convert <3%,. Cost: 18000 euros, 12 weeks.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Sample: 200 hobbyists and small workshop owners recruited via metalworking forums and social media, balanced by experience level (beginner, intermediate, advanced).. Measure: 1) Choice: premium-priced Gühring precision tool vs. generic alternative (20% price premium). 2) WTP: maximum price hobbyists would pay for a premium tool. 3) Single-source intent: likelihood to purchase a bundled kit of 10 tools (15% discount).. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 72 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Sample: 200 participants: 100 self‑identified hobbyists/small workshop owners (recruited via metalworking forums and social media) and 100 professionals (recruited via industry associations and LinkedIn). Randomly assign each participant to one of two message versions.. Measure: Average WTP (EUR) and average purchase intent score for each message version.. Predictions: T1: Hobbyists exposed to premium messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to professional messaging.; T2: Professionals exposed to professional messaging will show a higher average WTP and purchase intent than those exposed to premium messaging.. Decision rule: If the average WTP for premium messaging exceeds professional messaging by at least 15% (or purchase intent by at least 10 points on the 1‑10 scale) among hobbyists, proceed to develop a premium consumer proposition. T1: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects. Who benefits: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika can communicate that its products are designed for everyday use, are easy to apply, and deliver professional outcomes, consumers will shift from generic store‑brand sealants to Sika, reducing reliance on contractor‑only solutions.. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher retail margins on consumer‑branded items, direct‑to‑consumer sales, and brand extension into home improvement retail.. Assumptions: Consumers trust Sika’s professional reputation and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.; Retail distribution (e.g., hardware stores, online marketplaces) is accessible and cost‑effective for Sika.; Marketing can effectively communicate ease‑of‑use and professional results to DIY buyers.. Predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded DIY sealant at a price comparable to leading store‑brand sealants will achieve higher unit sales and repeat purchase rate among DIY shoppers compared to an identical product sold under a generic brand.; Surveyed DIY consumers will rate Sika’s product as “very easy to use” or “easy to use” at least 60% of the time, indicating perceived ease‑of‑application..

T2: Contractors will purchase Sika’s consumer products for residential projects because they need reliable, code‑compliant sealants and adhesives that can be used on both professional and personal jobs, reducing the need for separate supplier relationships. Who benefits: Contractors who work on both residential and commercial projects and value a single supplier for code‑compliant materials.. Why behaviour changes: If Sika offers a consumer‑branded line that meets residential building codes and is compatible with professional‑grade products, contractors can buy a single brand for both types of work, simplifying procurement and reducing inventory costs. How value is captured: Sika would capture value through higher volume sales to contractors, cross‑selling of professional and consumer lines, and reduced distribution costs by serving both B2B and B2C channels.. Assumptions: Contractors are willing to pay a premium for a single brand that meets both professional and residential standards.; Sika can produce consumer‑grade products that meet residential building codes without compromising professional performance.; Contractors are willing to purchase from Sika directly or through existing distribution channels.. Predictions: A test offering a Sika‑branded sealant marketed as “professional‑grade for residential use” will achieve higher purchase intent among contractors compared to a generic store‑brand sealant marketed only for residential use.; Surveyed contractors will indicate that they would use Sika’s consumer product for at least 30% of their residential projects, citing code compliance and convenience..

T1: Enthusiast motorcyclists will purchase premium Brembo brakes directly because they value performance and brand heritage, and are willing to pay a premium for proven motorsport technology. Who benefits: Brembo benefits by capturing higher-margin sales of premium brake kits to individual enthusiasts.. Why behaviour changes: Motorcyclists seek performance upgrades that demonstrate their passion and affiliation with professional racing; they trust Brembo's motorsport pedigree and are willing to pay more for a product that signals expertise.. How value is captured: Brembo sells directly to enthusiasts at premium prices, retaining the full retail margin rather than selling through intermediaries.. Assumptions: Motorcyclists have sufficient disposable income to afford premium brake upgrades.; Brand awareness of Brembo's motorsport history is strong among enthusiasts.; Direct-to-consumer sales channels are feasible and cost-effective for Brembo.. Predictions: If offered a premium Brembo brake kit priced at €750, at least 10% of surveyed enthusiasts will express intent to purchase.; Sales of the premium kit will generate higher per-unit revenue than aftermarket replacement parts..

T2: Consumers will purchase Brembo brakes for urban and everyday use because they seek reliable, high‑performance braking solutions that enhance safety and convenience, and are willing to pay a premium for a brand associated with quality and innovation. Who benefits: Brembo benefits by expanding its consumer base into urban and everyday segments, capturing higher‑margin sales of lifestyle‑branded kits and potentially licensing its technology to third‑party consumer brands.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers prioritize safety and performance in daily driving and urban mobility; they trust Brembo's reputation for engineering excellence and are willing to pay more for a product that signals modern, tech‑savvy lifestyle.. How value is captured: Brembo sells premium lifestyle kits directly or through licensed partners at higher prices, retaining margin and building brand equity beyond its core automotive B2B business.. Assumptions: Urban and everyday drivers have sufficient disposable income to afford premium brake upgrades.; Brand awareness of Brembo's technological leadership is growing among non‑motorcycle enthusiasts.; Lifestyle branding effectively communicates performance and heritage to non‑technical consumers.. Predictions: If offered a lifestyle‑branded Brembo brake kit priced at €300 for urban use, at least 15% of surveyed urban drivers will express intent to purchase.; Sales of the lifestyle kit will generate higher per‑unit revenue than standard aftermarket parts..

Does not show: The review does not show whether enthusiasts would purchase at that price, nor does it address willingness to pay for premium heritage-driven products..

Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Enthusiast vs Lifestyle Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a premium enthusiast brake kit priced at €750; Group B sees a lifestyle-branded brake kit priced at €300. Both groups are asked about purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (open‑ended).. Sample: 200 participants: 100 motorcycle enthusiasts (recruited via biker forums) and 100 urban drivers (recruited via general consumer panels).. Measure: Average purchase intent score for each group and the difference between the two groups.. Predictions: T1: Group A will show higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B.; T2: Group B will show higher average purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A.. Decision rule: If Group A’s average purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group B’s, T1 is supported. If Group B’s average purchase intent is at least 10 percentage points higher than Group A’s, T2 is supported. If the difference is less than 10 points, both theories remain uncertain.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting enthusiast motorcyclists, but first validate demand and willingness to pay through a low‑cost willingness‑to‑pay survey before committing to full product development or marketing. The survey will test whether enthusiasts are willing to pay €750 for a premium heritage‑branded brake kit, which would support T1, or whether a lower‑priced lifestyle kit would be, Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

T1 kept: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, willingness to pay, or enthusiast purchasing behavior. Therefore it neither supports nor contradicts T1. New claim: none. Evidence: SYN-D.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting enthusiast motorcyclists, but first validate demand and willingness to pay through a low‑cost willingness‑to‑pay survey before committing to full product development or marketing. Value proposition: A premium, heritage‑branded brake kit that combines Brembo’s motorsport pedigree with advanced adjustability and adjustability, sold directly to enthusiasts at a price point that reflects premium positioning.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed willingness‑to‑pay survey (200 participants, €15,000, 10 weeks) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for a €750 enthusiast kit versus a €300 lifestyle kit.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on consumer demand and willingness to pay for premium enthusiast kits. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows that at least 10% of enthusiasts express intent to purchase the €750 kit and willingness to pay that price, T1 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to full product development for enthusiasts.; If the survey shows that the €300 lifestyle kit generates higher intent and willingness to pay among enthusiasts, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to a broader urban/everyday consumer proposition.. T1: Private electric car drivers will purchase Lapp's electromobility accessories directly if they perceive a clear convenience benefit (e.g., simplified charging, faster installation) and can afford the price premium. Who benefits: Lapp Mobility GmbH gains consumer sales revenue and brand extension into the automotive aftermarket.. Why behaviour changes: Growing adoption of electric vehicles creates a market of private drivers seeking convenient charging solutions; competition among suppliers creates a price-sensitive environment that favors clear functional advantages.. How value is captured: Lapp can capture value by selling premium-priced, integrated charging solutions directly to consumers, leveraging its existing e-mobility product line and global logistics.. Assumptions: Private EV owners are willing to pay a premium for convenience and reliability.; Lapp can design and market a consumer-friendly charging kit that reduces installation time.; The company's sales network can reach private buyers effectively.. Predictions: In a test offering a simplified charging kit to private EV owners, purchase intent will be higher than a generic cable product.; Average willingness to pay will exceed the price of standard cables by at least 20%..

T2: Private electric car drivers will purchase Lapp's electromobility accessories if they receive incentives or subsidies from governments or utilities, making the price barrier lower. Method: Run two parallel pilot programs in two distinct consumer segments: (1) a convenience-focused group (e.g., apartment building residents) offered a digital refund app with deposit return; (2) an eco-focused group offered a sensor-sorted mixed-waste collection service. Decision rule: If digital refund adoption rate ≥ 15% AND eco-friendly adoption rate ≤ 10%, then T1 is supported. Test "Willingness-to-Pay Survey for High‑Performance Brake Kits" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated direct‑to‑consumer pricing. Decision rule: If average willingness‑to‑pay for enthusiasts exceeds €750 – €800, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting enthusiasts. If both averages fall below €750 – €800, recommend no expansion.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

T1: Consumers will adopt Lapp components in home automation and automotive aftermarket if the company offers a differentiated, premium-priced consumer proposition that emphasizes safety, reliability, and brand reputation from its industrial leadership. Who benefits: Lapp Mobility GmbH gains higher-margin consumer sales and brand extension into new markets.. Why behaviour changes: Consumers trust Lapp’s industrial reputation and seek reliable components for safety-critical applications (e.g., home charging, automotive connectivity). A differentiated proposition signals quality and reduces perceived risk.. How value is captured: Lapp captures value through premium pricing, direct-to-consumer sales channels, and brand licensing, leveraging existing manufacturing capacity and global logistics.. Assumptions: Consumers associate Lapp with industrial excellence and are willing to pay a premium for safety.; Lapp can design and market consumer-specific products without major redesign.; Distribution channels (e.g., online, specialty retailers) are accessible and cost-effective.. Predictions: If Lapp launches a consumer proposition with clear safety messaging, purchase intent among target consumers will be at least 15% higher than a generic industrial product.; Sales in the consumer segment will grow at a rate exceeding overall group sales growth within 12 months.; Brand perception surveys will show increased awareness of Lapp as a consumer brand among target demographics..

T2: Consumers will adopt Lapp components in home automation and automotive aftermarket if the company offers a differentiated, low-cost proposition that leverages its existing industrial volume production to reduce unit prices, making the product affordable for price-sensitive segments. Who benefits: Lapp Mobility GmbH gains volume sales and market penetration in consumer segments without sacrificing margins, while consumers benefit from lower prices.. Why behaviour changes: Price-sensitive consumers choose Lapp because its industrial scale lowers unit costs, making the product more affordable than competitors. This perceived value drives purchase decisions.. How value is captured: Lapp captures value through high-volume sales, economies of scale, and potentially volume licensing to consumer brands, while maintaining overall profitability.. Assumptions: Lapp can produce consumer components at the same cost structure as industrial components.; Price is a primary purchase driver for target consumers.; Distribution channels (e.g., mass retailers) are willing to stock Lapp at lower margins.. Predictions: If Lapp launches a consumer proposition with a 20% price reduction compared to competitors, unit sales will increase by at least 30% within 12 months.; Consumer surveys will show that price is the top reason for choosing Lapp over alternatives.; Average order value will remain stable or increase, indicating that volume drives revenue..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Premium vs Low-Cost Proposition" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with randomized exposure to either a premium-priced safety-focused proposition or a low-cost volume-focused proposition, followed by willingness-to-pay (WTP) and purchase intent questions.. Sample: 500 German consumers aged 25-55 who own or plan to purchase electric vehicles or home automation devices within 12 months, recruited via an online panel.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: "Would buy") and WTP (EUR). Secondary: brand perception (trust, safety perception) and price sensitivity.. Predictions: T1: Premium proposition will achieve at least 15% higher purchase intent and a WTP at least 10% above the low-cost proposition.; T2: Low-cost proposition will achieve at least 30% higher purchase intent and a WTP at least 20% below the premium proposition.. Decision rule: If premium purchase intent >= low-cost purchase intent + 15% AND premium WTP >= low-cost WTP + 10%, proceed with premium consumer proposition. If low-cost purchase intent >= premium purchase intent + 15% AND low-cost WTP >= premium WTP + 20%,. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes safety, reliability, and brand reputation from Lapp’s industrial leadership, targeting home automation and automotive aftermarket. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., a safety-focused charging kit for electric vehicles) and use the test results to decide on broader rollout. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes safety, reliability, and brand reputation from Lapp’s industrial leadership, targeting home automation and automotive aftermarket. Begin with a limited launch (e.g., a safety-focused charging kit for electric vehicles) and use the test results to decide on broader rollout. Target customer: Price-sensitive consumers in the home automation and automotive aftermarket who value safety and reliability, and are willing to pay a premium for Lapp’s industrial reputation.. Value proposition: A safety-focused, premium-priced consumer product leveraging Lapp’s industrial quality and brand trust, sold through direct-to-consumer channels to capture higher margins and build brand extension.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (500 German consumers, 10 weeks, €15,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness-to-pay for a premium safety proposition versus a low-cost volume proposition.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for Lapp components, the willingness of consumers to pay a premium for safety, and the competitive response from established consumer brands remain uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows the low-cost proposition outperforms the premium proposition by at least 15% in purchase intent and 20% in willingness-to-pay, we would reconsider a low-cost volume strategy.; If new evidence shows Lapp already sells significant consumer volumes through existing channels, we would focus on expanding existing B2B segments rather than creating a new consumer proposition.. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical brake kit, specifications, price, fitting service, warranty and delivery time. One offer included a free demo ride on a bike fitted with the brakes at a partner shop before ordering; the other showed the same kit with test reports and specification sheets. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the demo-ride offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether trying the product first changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, the cost of running demo rides, or how established bicycle-brake brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Survey for a Consumer-Grade Biesse CNC Router" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY woodworkers (defined as those who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months) and homeowners (defined as those who have undertaken home improvement projects requiring precision cutting). Each participant is shown a product description of a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router with specifications matching a desktop model (e.g., 12"x24" work. Sample: 200 participants: 100 DIY woodworkers and 100 homeowners. Recruitment via a panel provider to ensure geographic diversity.. Measure: Willingness-to-pay (WTP) in euros, measured as the maximum price participants would pay for the router. Secondary measures: purchase intent (binary) and perceived importance of precision and professional-grade features.. Predictions: T1: DIY woodworkers will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).; T2: Homeowners will report a WTP at least 1.5x the price of comparable consumer CNC routers (e.g., €2,500 vs €1,600).. Decision rule: If the average WTP for DIY woodworkers exceeds €2,000 and the average WTP for homeowners exceeds €2,000, both theories are considered supported. If only one group exceeds €2,000, the theory for that group is supported, and the other is rejected. If neither group exceeds €2,000, both theories are rejected.. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. The survey will provide real demand evidence and help decide whether to invest in a differentiated consumer proposition or pursue other options. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Conduct the proposed consumer willingness-to-pay survey (Test X1) to empirically test whether DIY woodworkers are willing to pay a premium for a consumer-grade Biesse CNC router. The survey will provide real demand evidence and help decide whether to invest in a differentiated consumer proposition or pursue other options. Target customer: DIY woodworkers who have built or modified wood projects in the past 12 months and are willing to purchase directly from Biesse.. Value proposition: A consumer-grade Biesse CNC router that delivers professional-grade precision and digital control, sold directly to DIY woodworkers at a premium price, capturing margin on hardware and software while offering accessories and service. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the 10‑week, €15,000 willingness‑to‑pay survey with 200 participants (100 DIY woodworkers, 100 homeowners). Analyze results against the decision rule to determine whether to proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition or explore. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct evidence on DIY woodworker demand and willingness to pay a premium for a consumer‑grade router. The survey will resolve this uncertainty.. Would change if: If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay below €2,000 for DIY woodworkers, T1 would be rejected and the recommendation would shift to other expansion options or no expansion.; If the survey shows average willingness‑to‑pay above €2,000 for homeowners, T2 would be supported and the recommendation would shift to targeting homeowners instead of DIY woodworkers.. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Hobbyist vs Fashion Pilot" between T1; T2. Method: Run two parallel pilot sales channels for a limited-edition, consumer-grade spinning kit: (1) Hobbyist channel targeting crafters via online craft communities and social media; (2) Fashion channel targeting small-scale fashion manufacturers via industry forums and design competitions. Both channels offer the same kit at a fixed price of €350, with optional accessories sold separately. Track the following metrics for 12 weeks:. Sample: Hobbyist channel: 200 crafters recruited via craft forums and social media. Fashion channel: 150 small-scale fashion designers recruited via industry forums and design competitions.. Measure: 1) Number of units sold per channel (total and per week). 2) Average order value (including accessories). 3) Customer satisfaction score (5-point scale). 4) Repeat purchase rate for accessories within 6 months.. Predictions: T1: Hobbyist channel will achieve at least 150 units sold and a repeat purchase rate of 30% for accessories, while the fashion channel will achieve fewer than 50 units sold.; T2: Fashion channel will achieve at least 100 units sold and a repeat purchase rate of 20% for accessories, while the hobbyist channel will achieve fewer than 50 units sold.. Decision rule: If the hobbyist channel sells ≥150 units and the fashion channel sells <50 units, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting hobbyists (support T1). If the fashion channel sells ≥100 units and the hobbyist channel sells <50 units, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting small-scale fashion manufacturers (support T2). If both channels meet. Cost: 20000 euros, 12 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, run the proposed Hobbyist vs Fashion pilot (Test X1) to empirically test demand for a home spinning kit. If the pilot confirms at least 150 units sold in the hobbyist channel and a 30% repeat purchase rate for accessories, proceed to develop a consumer proposition targeting hobbyists. If not, maintain the current B2B focus. The pilot cost is €20,000 Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Subscription vs Entry-Level CNC Test" between T1; T2. Method: Randomized controlled trial with two parallel groups. Group A receives a €2,000 entry-level CNC router with a limited warranty and optional accessories. Group B receives the same router plus a 12-month subscription that includes software updates, cloud storage, and remote support. Both groups are offered a 10% discount if they sign up for the subscription within 12 weeks. The test runs for 12 weeks, and participants are contacted weekly to assess purchase intent, . Sample: 200 DIY woodworkers recruited via woodworking forums, social media, and local workshops. 100 participants per group.. Measure: Purchase conversion rate (percentage of participants who buy the router) and subscription uptake rate (percentage of participants who subscribe to the service).. Predictions: T1: Group A purchase rate ≥ 30%, Group B purchase rate ≤ 15% (entry-level machine meets DIY needs).; T2: Group B subscription rate ≥ 40%, Group A subscription rate ≤ 20% (subscription model provides convenience and ongoing updates).. Decision rule: If Group A purchase rate ≥ 30% and Group B purchase rate ≤ 15%, proceed with developing a differentiated consumer proposition around entry-level machines. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Consumers will adopt Nabtesco’s existing automatic door technology as a differentiated consumer proposition if they perceive it as a safety and convenience upgrade for home entry, leading to premium pricing and repeat purchases. Who benefits: Homeowners seeking enhanced safety and convenience; Nabtesco benefits from higher-margin direct sales and brand extension into residential markets.. Why behaviour changes: Growing awareness of home security and accessibility needs creates demand for smart, automatic door solutions that reduce injury risk and improve user experience.. How value is captured: Nabtesco captures value through premium pricing for residential units, direct-to-consumer sales channels, and potential subscription services for software updates and remote control.. Assumptions: Consumers are willing to pay a premium for automatic doors that improve safety and convenience.; Nabtesco can adapt its existing automatic door technology for residential use without major redesign.; Distribution channels (e.g., online, retail partners) exist to reach individual buyers.. Predictions: A test offering the automatic door as a consumer product will achieve at least 10% higher average price than standard automatic doors.; Purchase intent among target homeowners will be at least 15% higher than for a generic automatic door proposition..

T2: Consumers will adopt Nabtesco’s existing automatic door technology as a differentiated consumer proposition primarily because they seek convenience and time savings in daily routines, leading to higher adoption rates in new-build homes and retrofits. Who benefits: Homeowners and builders who value time efficiency; Nabtesco benefits from volume sales and integration into residential construction pipelines.. Why behaviour changes: Growing urban populations and demand for smart homes create a market for automatic doors that reduce entry time and improve overall convenience.. How value is captured: Nabtesco captures value through bulk pricing for residential projects, partnerships with builders, and optional add‑on services such as remote control apps.. Assumptions: Consumers prioritize convenience over premium pricing in automatic door decisions.; Builders are willing to include automatic doors in new‑build projects if they reduce installation time.; Nabtesco can supply residential units at scale without redesigning the core technology.. Predictions: A test offering automatic doors as a convenience‑focused residential product will achieve at least 20% higher adoption rate among builders than a generic automatic door proposition.; Purchase intent among builders will be at least 15% higher when the proposition emphasizes time‑saving benefits..

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Safety vs Convenience Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants view two versions of a Nabtesco automatic door product description: (1) Safety/Rehabilitation version emphasizing enhanced safety and accessibility for users with limited mobility; (2) Convenience version emphasizing time savings and ease of use for homeowners. Participants indicate purchase intent (1‑10 scale) and willingness to pay (EUR).. Sample: 200 homeowners (100 per version) recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and geographic region.. Measure: Average willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent score (1‑10) for each version.. Predictions: T1: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the safety/rehabilitation version than for the convenience version.; T2: Higher willingness to pay and purchase intent for the convenience version than for the safety/rehabilitation version.. Decision rule: If the safety/rehabilitation version’s average willingness to pay exceeds the convenience version’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent score is at least 10 points higher, proceed with the safety/rehabilitation proposition. If the convenience version’s average willingness to pay exceeds the safety/rehabilitation version’s by at least €100 and its purchase intent score is at least 10 points higher, proceed with the convenience proposition. If neither. Cost: 15000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for safety/rehabilitation versus convenience messaging. If the test confirms a €100+ price difference and a 10-point purchase intent difference favoring safety/rehabilitation, proceed to develop a safety-focused automatic door proposition for home‑‑‑ Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition yet. Instead, conduct the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to measure willingness to pay and purchase intent for safety/rehabilitation versus convenience messaging. Value proposition: A Nabtesco automatic door that meets either safety/rehabilitation needs (enhanced stability and accessibility) or convenience needs (time-saving entry).. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the Consumer Preference Test (X1) within the €15,000 budget and 10‑week timeline, using the proposed methodology to compare willingness to pay and purchase intent for safety/rehabilitation versus convenience messaging.. Uncertainty: Both T1 and T2 remain uncertain due to lack of direct consumer demand data; the test is needed to resolve which driver (safety/rehabilitation vs convenience) drives higher willingness to pay and purchase intent.. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a machine at a price these buyers pay could be built, that the market is large enough, or that it fits the company's industrial dealers. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the application-kit offer and 72 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.
