sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 32 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "DIY Sealant Messaging Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants view a product description of a Sika DIY sealant (easy-apply, professional-grade) and are asked: "How likely are you to purchase this product?" (1‑10 scale). Measure: Average purchase likelihood score and average WTP for the easy‑apply version versus a control version described as a standard contractor‑grade sealant.. Predictions: T1: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 10% higher.; T2: Average purchase likelihood for easy‑apply version will be at least 20% higher than for control version, and WTP will be at least 15% higher.. Decision rule: If the easy‑apply version’s average likelihood exceeds the control version’s by ≥ 20 points AND the WTP premium is ≥ 10% (or ≥ 15% for T2), then the theory is supported. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 72 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

T1: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s precision tools if they perceive them as affordable, reliable, and compatible with existing CNC machines, because these attributes lower the perceived risk and cost of switching from other brands. Who benefits: Gühring benefits by capturing sales from a growing segment of individual buyers who value precision and compatibility, expanding its consumer market beyond B2B.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists view Gühring as a trusted, compatible alternative that performs as well as higher‑priced competitors, they will purchase it instead of cheaper alternatives or continue using existing tools.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its tools competitively while maintaining its premium reputation, generating revenue from a new consumer segment without diluting its industrial brand.. Assumptions: Hobbyists and small workshops have sufficient budget for precision tools.; They prioritize reliability and compatibility over cost.; They are aware of Gühring through existing B2B channels or word of mouth.. Predictions: If offered at a price 10‑20% below premium CNC tool brands, Gühring will achieve at least 5% market share among hobbyists within 12 months.; Customer surveys will show that compatibility with existing CNC machines is the top purchase driver for 60% of buyers..

T2: Hobbyists and small workshops will adopt Gühring’s tools if they are marketed as a premium, status‑enhancing brand that signals expertise and craftsmanship, because status motivates purchase decisions beyond functional need. Who benefits: Gühring benefits by commanding premium prices and building a consumer brand that differentiates it from generic tools, potentially creating a new revenue stream while preserving its industrial reputation.. Why behaviour changes: If hobbyists perceive Gühring as a brand that signifies high‑quality craftsmanship and expert use, they will choose it over cheaper alternatives even if the tools serve the same functional purpose.. How value is captured: Gühring can price its consumer line at a premium (e.g., 20‑30% above generic CNC tools) while leveraging its existing industrial reputation to justify the price, generating higher margins from a new consumer segment.. Assumptions: Hobbyists value brand status and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.; They are exposed to Gühring through its industrial presence and may seek out the brand for its reputation.; They differentiate between tools based on brand perception rather than purely functional performance.. Predictions: If marketed as a premium brand, Gühring will achieve at least 3% market share among hobbyists within 12 months, with average price paid 20% above generic alternatives.; Surveyed hobbyists will rank brand status as the top purchase driver for 40% of buyers..

Test "Hobbyist Purchase Driver Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online choice-based conjoint survey with a sample of 300 hobbyists (recruited via CNC forums and metalworking communities). Participants view two Gühring product variants: a standard precision drill bit priced at 120 € (equivalent to a premium CNC tool price point) and a premium-branded variant priced at 180 € (20% above the standard price). Both variants are described as compatible with their existing CNC machine and marketed with the same functional description (e.g., “. Sample: 300 hobbyists (150 per variant) recruited via CNC forums and metalworking communities.. Measure: Purchase intent (binary: “Would buy”) and willingness to pay (WTP) difference between the two variants.. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the standard variant (120 €) because hobbyists prioritize affordability and compatibility.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP for the premium variant (180 €) because hobbyists value brand status and are willing to pay a premium for perceived quality.. Decision rule: If the purchase intent for the premium variant exceeds the standard variant by at least 10 percentage points AND the average WTP for the premium variant is at least €20 higher than the standard variant, then the evidence supports T2 (premium branding). If the premium variant exceeds the standard by  . Cost: 15000 euros, 8 weeks.

In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks, hunters and anglers interested in a chamber vacuum sealer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer stated that the machine uses plain chamber pouches costing a fraction of embossed bags and showed the yearly bag cost for typical use; the other showed the same machine and listed the pouch type without a cost comparison. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 reservations for the running-cost offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether running costs change choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at the machine's price, that the household market is large enough, or that it would sustain a consumer business beside the industrial one. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Preference Test: Professional-Grade vs. Time-Saving Messaging" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either professional-grade performance messaging (T1) or time-saving convenience messaging (T2). Participants view a product mockup and a brief description of the proposed consumer vacuum sealer. They then indicate purchase intent on a 1‑10 scale and willingness to pay (WTP) on a 1‑100 € scale.. Sample: 300 German home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking frequency.. Measure: Average purchase intent score (1‑10) and average WTP (1‑100 €).. Predictions: T1: Higher purchase intent and WTP when exposed to professional-grade messaging.; T2: Higher purchase intent and WTP when exposed to time-saving messaging.. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the professional-grade group exceeds the time-saving group by at least 1.5 points (e.g., 7.5 vs. 6) AND the average WTP for the professional-grade group exceeds the time-saving group by at least €20, then T1 is supported. If the opposite. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Run the proposed consumer preference test (X1) to empirically compare purchase intent and willingness to pay under professional-grade versus time-saving messaging. The test will provide evidence on which messaging frame drives consumer adoption, enabling a data-driven decision on whether to develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case. Beliefs: T1: uncertain; T2: uncertain.

Evidence: SYN-MULTIVAC-UPDATE.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 letters of intent for the rental offer and 32 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical products, charging power, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added a free check of the owner's car model and home wiring with a written assurance that the set would work with both; the other listed the same compatibility tables for the owner to check. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small workshops, shops and garages were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact automated storage module. Both showed the identical machine, capacity, installation, service and total cost over five years. One offer was a monthly rental with service included and no upfront payment; the other was an outright purchase with the same service contract. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a signed letter of intent not withdrawn after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 letters of intent for the rental offer and 72 for the purchase offer. This tests whether the upfront cost changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a module small and cheap enough could be built, that installation and service would pay at this scale, or that private households would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited camper-van and motorhome owners interested in a diesel parking heater were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical heater, brand, heat output, total installed price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included fitting by a certified mobile technician at the owner's home on a booked date; the other required the owner to book the same fitting at a dealer workshop. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the mobile-fitting offer and 72 for the workshop offer. This tests whether installation friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at today's prices, that mobile fitting can be staffed or earns a margin, or that it would win buyers from cheaper self-fitted heaters. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby spinners and small fibre-farm owners interested in a compact electric spinning machine were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical machine, output, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer included two live training sessions with a spinning instructor and a setup visit; the other included the same machine with a printed manual and video links. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the instructor-onboarding offer and 72 for the manual-only offer. This tests whether the skill barrier changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that a spinning-machine maker could build such a machine at a price these buyers pay, that the hobby market is large enough, or that it would fit an industrial business. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited older home owners and family members considering an automatic opener for a home entrance door were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed the identical opener, installation, price, warranty and delivery time. One offer added an independent safety certificate for the door's anti-pinch sensors and an in-home demonstration of the door stopping on contact; the other showed the same opener with its specification sheet. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the safety-assurance offer and 32 for the specification-only offer. This tests whether safety assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand at this price beyond that group, that installers would carry the product, or why a rival's home opener left the market. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited mountain-bike and e-bike riders considering a premium brake upgrade were assigned equally to two offers. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited hobby 3D-printer owners were assigned equally to two offers for the same diamond-tipped nozzle. Both showed the identical product, price, compatibility list, delivery time and return policy. One offer added a written wear guarantee with a free replacement if the nozzle wore out within two years of printing abrasive filament; the other described the same nozzle as wear resistant without a guarantee. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the guaranteed offer and 32 for the standard offer. This tests whether a durability assurance changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show how many hobbyists print abrasive filament, what the guarantee would cost the company, or that cutting-tool customers would follow. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 32 deposits for the template-software offer and 72 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. sources.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home owners planning to reseal a bathroom or window were assigned equally to two offers for the same sealant. Both showed the identical product, colour range, cure time, price, shelf life and return policy. One offer was a kit with a smoothing tool, masking tape and a step-by-step guide for a clean finish; the other was the same cartridge with the standard label instructions. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the application-kit offer and 32 for the cartridge-only offer. This tests whether application difficulty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the margin on a kit, how retailers would stock it, or that DIY volumes would matter beside professional sales. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "DIY vs Contractor Purchase Intent Test" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Participants are recruited from a panel of DIY enthusiasts and professional contractors. They are shown a Sika-branded DIY sealant description (easy-to-use, affordable, professional-grade results) and a Sika-branded contractor sealant description (code-compliant, single supplier for both residential and commercial, reduces inventory costs). They are asked to indicate on a 1‑10 scale how likely they are to purchase each product for a. Sample: 300 participants: 150 DIY (recruited via hobbyist forums and social media) and 150 contractors (recruited via professional associations and construction industry platforms).. Measure: Purchase intent score for each product (1‑10 scale). Secondary measure: willingness to pay (EUR) for each product.. Predictions: T1: DIY participants will rate the DIY product as at least 7/10 and the contractor product as 5/10 or lower, indicating they prefer the consumer-branded product for their own projects. Contractors will rate both products similarly (e.g., 6/10 for both).; T2: Contractors will rate the contractor product as at least 7/10 and the DIY product as 5/10 or lower, indicating they prefer the professional-branded product for both residential and commercial use. DIY participants will rate both products similarly.. Decision rule: If the average DIY purchase intent score for the DIY product is at least 7 and the contractor product is 5 or lower, proceed with a differentiated consumer proposition targeting DIY. If the contractor product score is at least 7 and the DIY product is 5 or lower, . Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.

Favours T1: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts, emphasizing ease of use, affordability, and professional-grade results. Begin with a limited launch of a Sika-branded DIY sealant in select retail channels, using the evidence that Sika already offers a DIY range and that DIY spending remains stable despite pandemic-related shifts. Beliefs: T1: likely; T2: uncertain.

It does not address contractors or code compliance, so it does not affect T2. The test shows a higher purchase rate for the kit (72) than for the cartridge (32), supporting T1’s premise that perceived ease of use drives DIY consumer choice. New claim: Homeowners will purchase Sika’s consumer products if they perceive them as easy‑to‑use, affordable, and offering professional‑grade results, because they value convenience and cost‑effectiveness for DIY projects.. Evidence: SYN-SIKA-UPDATE.

Recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts, emphasizing ease of use, affordability, and professional-grade results. Begin with a limited launch of a Sika-branded DIY sealant in select retail channels, using the evidence that Sika already offers a DIY range and that DIY spending remains stable despite pandemic-related shifts. Target customer: Individual homeowners and DIY enthusiasts who need reliable sealants, adhesives, or waterproofing for home improvement projects.. Value proposition: A Sika-branded DIY sealant that delivers professional-grade results while being easy to apply and affordable, allowing consumers to achieve professional outcomes without contractor intervention.. Favoured theory: T1. Next action: Run the proposed DIY vs Contractor Purchase Intent Test (300 participants, 10 weeks, €18,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the consumer-branded product versus the professional-branded product.. Uncertainty: The size of the consumer market for Sika’s DIY products, the willingness of DIY shoppers to pay a premium for a Sika brand, and the competitive response from established consumer sealant brands remain uncertain.. Would change if: If the test shows the contractor product achieving at least 7/10 purchase intent and the DIY product below 5/10, we would shift focus to a contractor-focused proposition (T2).; If DIY participants consistently rate both products similarly (e.g., 6/10) without a clear preference, we would reconsider expansion.; If new evidence shows Sika’s DIY products are already sold through major retailers with strong consumer demand, we would prioritize scaling existing distribution rather than creating a new brand.. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited owners of small carpentry workshops and skilled hobby woodworkers were assigned equally to two offers for the same compact CNC router. Both showed the identical machine, working area, price, installation, warranty and delivery time. One offer came with simplified design software and a library of ready-to-cut furniture templates that need no programming; the other came with the standard professional CAD/CAM software. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a paid refundable deposit remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 deposits for the template-software offer and 32 for the standard-software offer. This tests whether programming complexity changes choice in that recruited group. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited private electric-car owners shopping for a home charging cable and wallbox were assigned equally to two offers. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. The outcome was a completed purchase not returned within 30 days among all 400 assigned people per arm. There were 72 purchases for the checked-compatibility offer and 32 for the self-checked offer. This tests whether compatibility uncertainty changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show demand beyond that group, the cost of running the checks, or how established wallbox brands would respond. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow mechanism changes.

Test "Consumer Purchase Intent Test: Performance Advantage vs Retail Channel" between T1; T2. Method: Online survey with randomized exposure to either a performance‑focused vacuum sealer ad (highlighting professional‑grade sealing performance) or a retail‑focused ad (highlighting availability in specialty kitchen stores). Participants are asked about purchase intent and willingness to pay.. Sample: 500 home cooks and culinary enthusiasts recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and cooking experience.. Measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7‑point scale ("Very unlikely" to "Very likely"). Secondary measure: maximum price participants would pay (WTP).. Predictions: T1: Participants exposed to the performance‑focused ad will report higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a premium (e.g., at least 15% higher than a comparable consumer‑grade sealer).; T2: Participants exposed to the retail‑focused ad will report higher purchase intent and be willing to pay a comparable price (e.g., at least 10% higher than a similar sealer sold only online).. Decision rule: If the average purchase intent for the performance‑focused group exceeds the retail‑focused group by at least 15 percentage points (or WTP by at least €30), T1 is supported. If the retail‑focused group exceeds the performance‑focused group by at least 15 percentage points, T2 is supported. If neither. Cost: 18000 euros, 10 weeks.
